claims: A landmine squat uses a barbell constrained around a fixed pivot; rack position, stance, support, foot movement, lower-body action, press action, path, and repetition boundary remain identity-critical.
{{canonicalName}} must declare whether the athlete faces toward or away from the pivot, where the sleeve is supported, whether the feet remain fixed, and whether a press is part of the repetition.
Squat, stationary split squat, and stepping lunge tasks differ in base of support, laterality, joint contribution, and repetition boundary.
Stance width and length, rack, hand count, arm-leg relationship, foot elevation, step direction, depth, tempo, range, load, and press timing are controlled dimensions.
Landmine squat loading involves the quadriceps, hamstrings and hip extensors with forces influenced by the anchored loading direction.
Record foot, ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, spine, trunk and grip contributions; add shoulder, scapular and elbow contributions only when the exact variant supports or presses the sleeve.
Landmine and goblet squat conditions produce different muscle activity and ground-reaction-force components, so implement geometry and body position cannot be treated as interchangeable.
Observable gates include a secure pivot, repeatable stance and distance, owned depth, foot-knee-pelvis control, declared rack, controlled ascent and a planned return or set-down.
Lower-limb joint angles, moments and ground-reaction forces differ across squat and lunge tasks, supporting exact-variant assessment.
Score exercise complexity and physical difficulty independently for each exact variant; derive overall difficulty as their maximum. Exercise cards contain no athlete skill or proficiency level.
Resistance-training stress depends on load, volume, effort, exercise selection, frequency and progression.
{{canonicalName}} can contribute quadriceps, gluteal, adductor, hamstring, calf, trunk and grip fatigue; press variants also add shoulder, upper-chest, triceps and scapular fatigue.
Landmine work requires a stable rated anchor, compatible barbell and loading hardware, and clear space for the complete bar and plate arc.
Declare floor traction, collars, plates, sleeve support, stance or step lane, pickup, return, set-down, coach position and the moving-bar exclusion zone.
Training outcomes depend on sets, repetitions, load, effort, frequency and recovery rather than the exercise name alone.
Use dose and rest that preserve the exact stance or step, depth, rack, path, side balance, action order and controlled return.
Instruction must separate equipment setup, rack transfer, stance or step, descent, bottom position, ascent, optional press, return and set-down.
The athlete and coach must know which foot or side leads, what depth counts, where pressure is maintained, when the press begins, and how a failed repetition is ended.
Qualified supervision, manageable resistance, correct technique, suitable equipment and gradual progression are core safeguards for resistance exercise.

Stop for pain, neurologic symptoms, dizziness, anchor or collar movement, plate shift, lost foot pressure, uncontrolled knee or pelvic motion, balance loss, trunk collapse, grinding, collision risk or loss of the planned return.
Exercise selection and resistance-training dose should be individualized to the intended adaptation, current capacity and recovery context.
Place heavy or high-coordination landmine squat and lunge work before material lower-body, pressing, grip or conditioning fatigue when strength, force or action quality is the priority.
The athlete needs the exact rack, stance, distance from pivot, hand count, side or step sequence, depth, load, repetitions, rest and stop signal.
Reduce load, range, velocity or support demand rather than silently changing from a stationary split squat to a stepping lunge or from a squat to a press combination.
The anchored resistance gives coaches observable setup, loading-direction, stance, path, range and finish checkpoints.
Coach support should expose anchor, collars, plate clearance, rack, stance, distance, side, step, depth, alignment, press timing, symptoms, dose, fatigue and shutdown actions.
Resistance exercise can be individualized through load, volume, range, effort, equipment and progression while preserving the intended task.

Options include a lighter or unloaded bar, reduced owned depth, fewer repetitions, longer rest, floor markers, a stable external support, written or audio cues, still images and live instruction; substitutions require reviewed identities.
Stationary split squats and stepping lunges have different start, support and repetition boundaries; a press adds an upper-body action and force-transfer demand.
Rack, hand count, attachment and arm-leg relationship can be exact variants inside a fixed action sequence; foot elevation, stepping, added press, rotation, jump or clean can change identity.
YouTube documents privacy-enhanced embedding, but a discovered watch URL does not prove current embed permission or exact exercise match.
The listed public-search candidates are unverified. Playback, oEmbed, embedding, exact-variant, cue, safety, caption, accessibility, quality, reviewer and approval checks remain unresolved.

assessmentSummary.identity: A bilateral squat performed facing a rated landmine pivot while supporting the sleeve at a declared central chest rack, descending to an owned depth and standing through the fixed diagonal arc before returning to the same rack.
currentCardFindings: The existing card uses generic landmine language and does not lock the central rack, pivot distance, stance, depth, path or safe transfer and set-down.
Migration 391 preserves Landmine Front Squat as distinct from free-weight Front Squat because the fixed pivot changes implement geometry, force direction, path, grip and failure response.
Migration 389 preserves the front-supported squat as distinct from Landmine Hack Squat, whose sleeve is supported behind or beside the shoulder while facing away from the pivot.

variantDifficultyCandidates.basis: central two-hand support reduces asymmetry while retaining fixed-pivot distance and rack-control demands
one-shoulder support adds anti-rotation, side balance and side-dose requirements while the feet remain bilateral

proposedDeliveryProfiles.purpose: Build bilateral squat strength and load tolerance through a repeatable anchored front-supported path.
Rehearse stance, pivot distance, rack, depth and alignment under low fatigue.

coach: Verify anchor, collars, load, central rack, stance, pivot distance, target depth and set-down plan.
Require whole-foot pressure, tracked knees, owned depth and a repeatable path relative to the pivot.
End the set when depth, stance, rack, alignment or return changes.
athlete: Hold the sleeve at the center of your chest, set your distance and brace.
Squat between your feet while keeping the rack connected and knees tracking with the toes.
Drive the floor away, finish tall and return the sleeve under control.

assessmentSummary.identity: A bilateral squat performed facing away from a rated landmine pivot with the sleeve supported beside the upper trapezius or shoulder, feet positioned forward to follow the fixed arc, descending to an owned depth and driving up and back before a controlled rerack.
currentCardFindings: The existing card does not declare away-from-pivot orientation, sleeve side, shoulder contact, foot position, rack transfer, depth or safe exit.

The shoulder side must alternate across matched sets or be explicitly dose-balanced; a machine hack squat does not share the free sleeve and landmine-pivot setup.

assessmentSummary.identity: A unilateral landmine combination beginning from a bilateral stance and declared shoulder rack, stepping the declared leg backward into a controlled reverse lunge, driving through the front leg to return toward standing while pressing through the fixed diagonal arc, then lowering to the same rack.
currentCardFindings: The existing card does not lock the working arm, step-back leg, front leg, press timing, start and finish stance, depth, return or side-dose accounting.
The canonical candidate defines the press during the drive back toward standing; pressing during the step-back descent is a different ordered-action proposal and is not silently accepted.
Landmine Split Squat keeps the feet fixed and has no required press; Landmine Squat-to-Press uses a bilateral squat rather than a step-back lunge.

variantDifficultyCandidates.basis: working arm and step-back leg share a side while the opposite front leg drives the return and press
cross-body arm and step-back pairing increase anti-rotation, balance and coaching demand

proposedDeliveryProfiles.purpose: Build repeatable side-specific lower-to-upper strength through the exact step-back, return and press sequence.
Express a crisp front-leg drive into the anchored press at low volume before timing degrades.

coach: Verify anchor, collars, load, working arm, step-back leg, markers, press timing, side sequence and set-down plan.
Require a controlled step and lunge, whole front-foot pressure, tracked knee and continuous drive toward standing into the press.
End the set when step, alignment, timing, speed, balance, finish or return changes.
athlete: Start square with the sleeve at the called shoulder and the called leg ready to step back.
Step back under control, own the lunge, then drive through the front foot and carry that return into the press.
Finish balanced, lower to the same shoulder and reset your feet before the next rep.

claims: Reverse-lunge joint angles, moments and forces differ from single-leg squat and forward-lunge tasks, supporting explicit step direction and side-dose accounting.
